items.title: Arthur "Monk" Hazel Interview, 1967-10-28
items.q: Buddy Rich was, uh, I was with Sharky at the time, at the Dream Room, and we were doubling with Buddy Rich.

ctx.x: Our guest tonight is Monk Hazel, who is celebrating his 50th year in jazz as a drummer, melophonist, trombone, cornet, what else? You didn't get around to any of this, huh? How has jazz drumming changed since you began, Monk?

Well, it's changed all, it's changed, it's a different thing altogether. And that, Cooper is the one who started all that. Because, you see, when we started, we were taught that the drums were supposed to be felt and not heard. And the most you ever took was a two or a four bar break. A solo, you know what you call a solo, they call them solos now. There was never no drum solos like you have today. Because if you didn't come up and did that, they'd run you off the stand. items.title: Arthur "Monk" Hazel Interview, 1959-07-16
items.q: I've had more drummers, you know, come in and look up like Krupa or Buddy Rich and those guys coming, they look up there and they're trying to figure out what I was doing

ctx.x: I play half and half. I play right-footed and left-handed. See, I originally started all left. See? And then, I don't know, it was more, my right leg was better. I could keep better time with the right leg than I could with the left. And then you didn't, we didn't have those flying horse things then, you know. And so I got, I don't know how I ever did it.
